analysis.one_liner: Requires online prescription drug sellers to disclose their identity, pharmacists, and licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 9 House Democrats in August 1999, sent to a Commerce Committee subcommittee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any website selling prescription drugs to post a clearly linked page identifying the business, its pharmacists and any online medical consultants, and the states where each is licensed. Sites that failed to do so could not legally sell prescription drugs. States with equally strict rules would handle enforcement for purchases made from within them.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy prescription drugs online, who would be able to see who they are buying from, whether the pharmacist is licensed, and where, before sending money or medical information to an unknown website.

how_it_helps.text: Any site used to sell prescription drugs would have to display the seller's name, business address, and phone number, and list every state where it is authorized to dispense drugs [S3].

The site would have to name each pharmacist and each online medical consultant, the states where they are licensed, and their professions, with a clearly visible link labeled 'licensing' or 'licenses' on every page [S3].

Selling prescription drugs through a non-compliant site would become a prohibited act under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, enforceable by the FDA and by states with equally strict rules [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Internet pharmacies, including online medical consultation services, would bear the cost of building and maintaining disclosure pages and could lose sales if they operate without proper state licenses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet pharmacies and online drug sellers

drawbacks.text: Disclosure does not stop the underlying problem of prescriptions issued without a real medical exam; a site could meet the disclosure rules and still sell drugs based on thin online consultations [S3].

The bill relies on state licensing disclosures and state or FDA enforcement, so sites hosted overseas or operating outside licensed states could remain out of reach, and the small states' primary enforcement role depends on each state adopting equally strict rules [S2][S3].
Compliance costs would fall on legitimate online pharmacies, and the definitions written for 1999 web technology (pages, links, protocol numbers) could age poorly as the internet changed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure requirement is a modest, low-cost consumer protection: it targets the cloak of anonymity that made early online drug sales risky, while leaving compliant pharmacies free to operate. Its limits are real — it does not require an in-person exam before prescribing and it reaches mainly sites within reach of US or state enforcement — but as a floor for transparency it weighed clearly on the side of consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee, then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2001 without any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Klink introduced the bill on August 5, 1999, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors including John Dingell, Henry Waxman, and Bart Stupak [S1][S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the same day, and on September 10, 1999, to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill died there when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, never having received a subcommittee vote, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online drug sellers continued operating without any federal disclosure obligation, and consumers who bought prescription drugs online remained without the identity and licensing information the bill would have guaranteed.

for.name: Rep. Ron Klink

for.role: Cosponsor; ranking Democrat on the Commerce Committee (MI)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding weight from the committee that controlled its fate.

for.role: Cosponsors (Stupak, Waxman, Green of Texas, Brady, Kanjorski, Doyle)

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 106th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after referring it to the Health and Environment Subcommittee on September 10, 1999; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so opposition never registered on the record; all nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee that let the bill sit was run by Republicans.

industries.industry: Internet pharmacies and online drug sellers
industries.note: Sites selling prescription drugs would have had to post their identity, pharmacists, and state licenses or lose the legal ability to sell. Sellers profiting from anonymity — especially those without valid licenses — would have lost that business model.
Disclosure of which states each online pharmacist is licensed in would level the field between web sellers and licensed local pharmacies, whose credentials customers can see in person.
